overview.text: Syphilis is a bacterial sexually transmitted infection caused by Treponema pallidum; it matters because, although curable, untreated infection can persist and cause serious damage. It usually spreads through direct contact with infectious sores during vaginal, anal, or oral sex, and can pass from a pregnant person to a fetus. The illness is described in primary, secondary, latent, and tertiary stages: an often painless sore called a chancre may appear first, followed by a sometimes faint rash, often on the palms or soles. Symptoms can disappear during latent infection. Years later, some untreated cases affect the heart, brain, or nervous system. Testing is important because signs may go unnoticed; antibiotics can cure the infection, though not always reverse damage.

key_facts.text: The bacterium Treponema pallidum causes syphilis, a sexually transmitted infection.
Syphilis can spread through direct contact with sores during vaginal, anal, or oral sex, and from a pregnant person to a fetus.
Its stages are primary, secondary, latent, and tertiary. The first may feature a painless chancre; secondary syphilis may cause a rash, including on the palms or soles.
Latent syphilis may have no visible signs; some untreated infections later damage the heart, brain, or nervous system.
Syphilis is curable with appropriate antibiotics, but treatment may not undo damage already caused by the infection.
